Always measure distances using the printed graphic scale bar on the map margin—graphic bars stay accurate even if a sheet is enlarged or reduced on a printer, whereas ruler ratios break when scaled.

Select a **handrail**—a continuous linear feature running alongside your intended direction (trail, stream edge, ridge crest, lakeshore, powerline or road)—to follow smoothly without staring constantly at a compass.

Check terrain hazards on both handrails and backstops: never use a frozen lake surface, active railroad track or flash-flood canyon floor as a walking handrail.

Watch for the classic warm-front cloud progression: high wispy cirrus thickening and lowering steadily into milky cirrostratus (often ringing sun/moon), then gray altostratus and finally low rain-bearing nimbostratus over 12–24 hours.

Watch for fast-moving cold-front cues: rapidly darkening western/northwestern cloud lines, sharp wind shifts, gusty outflow air and sudden steep temperature drops with brief heavy squalls or snow showers.
Treat visual sky reading strictly as an early-warning supplement to official NWS forecasts and NOAA Weather Radio—not a replacement for official watches and warnings.

Set FOUR objective abort limits before starting: (1) **Resource limit** (half water in deserts, fuel reserve in winter, half battery/daylight), (2) **Weather/Water limit** (active Warnings, lightning, whiteout, Gale/Small Craft Advisory, rising tide/creek).

Set (3) **Terrain/Hazard limit** (avalanche red flags, unverified ice, quaking bog, burn-scar storm, sneaker surf), and (4) **Human limit** (any signs of hypothermia, frostbite, heat stroke, HAPE/HACE, cold shock or group separation).
Treat ANY single crossed limit as an automatic group turnaround or shelter/evacuation trigger—never vote to "push just a little farther" past an objective life-safety threshold.
